title: Cluster-wide authz gates need identity-type check, not just namespace-scope check
answers: Why do we check identity type and namespace scope separately for cluster-wide reads?
Can an on-behalf-of user bypass the service-only gate by having namespace '*'?
What breaks if I simplify the cluster-wide list-keys check to just wildcard scope?
body:
Invariant: a gate restricting a cross-namespace read to service callers must check BOTH claims.IsIdentityType(info.GetIdentityType(), claims.TypeAccessPolicy) AND info.GetNamespace() == wildcardNamespace, enforced together in pkg/registry/apis/keys/handler.go:requireClusterWideServiceCaller.
Why: on-behalf-of requests copy the service token's namespace onto an identity typed as the end user, so a non-service user can legitimately hold the wildcard namespace scope. Combined with app-plugin kinds that defer authorization to storage (which can allow whole groups outside its RBAC allowlist), scope alone would let such a user enumerate object metadata across every tenant namespace.
Constraints: per-item/storage authorization is not a backstop here, so this check cannot be reduced to the namespace-scope check alone; any future refactor of this gate must keep both conditions, and a reviewer/mutation test should fail if either one is dropped.
applies: pkg/registry/apis/keys handlers that gate on cluster-wide (wildcard-namespace) reads; relevant to any similar on-behalf-of-aware authz gate
says: Why check both identity type and namespace scope for cluster-wide operations?
Can a delegated user bypass service-only restrictions by having wildcard scope?
What breaks if we only check namespace scope for cluster-wide reads?
How do we prevent delegated users from accessing restricted cross-namespace resources?
Why is identity type check required alongside namespace scope validation?
